lesson.title: CSMA/CA: Avoiding Collisions You Cannot Hear
lesson.summary: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance, the access method underlying Wi-Fi, substitutes explicit avoidance measures, interframe spacing, random backoff, and often RTS and CTS signaling, for the collision detection that wireless radios cannot reliably perform while transmitting.
lesson.body:
CSMA/CD's whole mechanism depends on a station being able to listen to the medium and detect a collision while it is still transmitting. On a wireless radio, that generally does not work: a station's own transmitter overwhelms its own receiver at close range, so it cannot reliably hear a faint colliding signal from another station arriving at the same time it is sending its own. Since collisions cannot be detected as they happen, CSMA/CA takes the opposite strategy: try much harder to avoid them before they occur, since discovering them after the fact by way of a missing acknowledgment is comparatively expensive on a wireless link with limited bandwidth.

The first avoidance mechanism is a mandatory pause before transmitting even onto an idle channel. After sensing the medium idle, a station waits a fixed interframe space, and then a random backoff interval counted down in discrete slot times, before actually transmitting. If the channel becomes busy again during the countdown, the station freezes its backoff counter and resumes counting down from where it left off once the channel is idle again. This spreads out the instants at which contending stations start transmitting, lowering the chance that two of them begin at exactly the same moment even when both were waiting for the same channel to clear.

The second mechanism addresses a problem specific to wireless that wired CSMA never faces: the hidden terminal problem. Picture stations A and C on either side of access point B, far enough apart that A and C cannot hear each other's radio transmissions at all, though both can hear B. A senses the channel, finds it idle, since from its own vantage point C's transmission is inaudible, and transmits to B, unaware that C might be transmitting to B at that same moment. The two signals collide at B even though neither A nor C ever detected anything wrong locally. CSMA/CA addresses this with an optional request to send and clear to send exchange: A first sends a short RTS frame to B, B replies with a CTS frame, and critically, that CTS is heard by every station within range of B, including C, which then knows to stay silent for the duration A has reserved, even though C never heard A's RTS directly.

Because collisions cannot be detected mid transmission, CSMA/CA leans on positive acknowledgment, the same ARQ pattern used throughout reliable link protocols, to confirm success after the fact rather than during it: the receiver sends an explicit ACK frame after successfully receiving a data frame, and if the sender does not receive that ACK within a timeout, it assumes a collision or corruption occurred, increases its contention window for backoff, a form of the same escalating randomization idea behind CSMA/CD's exponential backoff, and retries.

This layered approach, carrier sensing, mandatory spacing and random backoff, optional RTS and CTS reservation, and mandatory acknowledgments, is why Wi-Fi's real world throughput sits meaningfully below its advertised radio data rate even with no other traffic present: every one of those steps adds overhead that a wired CSMA/CD network, with its ability to detect and abort collisions cheaply and quickly, never had to pay in the same way.
